lead: Paul is stoned and left for dead at Lystra, gets up, and goes on. The journey ends where it began, at Antioch, with a report: God had opened a door of faith for the Gentiles. In the Gospel Jesus leaves his peace with men who are about to be badly shaken. Psalm 145 lets the friends of the Lord speak of the glory of his kingdom, the kingdom that Paul says we enter through many persecutions.

r.h: A door of faith for the Gentiles
set: The crowd that wanted to worship Paul yesterday is turned against him today. Opponents from Antioch of Pisidia and Iconium, where Paul had already met resistance, arrive and stir up the people. Luke means particular opponents from those cities; at Iconium a great number of Jews had in fact believed (14:1). Paul himself later recalls, “Once I received a stoning” (2 Corinthians 11:25), and 2 Timothy 3:11 recalls his sufferings at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra. Timothy came from Lystra (16:1).

After Derbe the apostles do not take the short road home through Tarsus. They go back the way they came, through the very towns that had driven them out, to strengthen the new believers. Then they sail home to Antioch in Syria, the church that had sent them out (13:1–3).
str: vv. 19–20: Paul is stoned, rises, and goes to Derbe.
vv. 21–23: the return journey: strengthening, encouraging, appointing elders.
vv. 24–26: the way back to Antioch.
vv. 27–28: the report to the church.
kw: Literally pressure, being pressed hard. Paul does not promise new Christians an easy road (v. 22). Suffering is not a sign that God has failed; it is part of the way into his kingdom.
Originally to stretch out the hand, as in voting; then simply to appoint. The apostles leave behind a recognised ministry in each church, with prayer and fasting (v. 23).
God opened it; the apostles only walked through it. Paul uses the same picture of an open door for the Gospel (1 Corinthians 16:9).
vv: Then they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.
Saul once guarded the coats of those who stoned Stephen (7:58). Now he knows the stones himself.
“It is through many persecutions that we must enter the kingdom of God.”
This is not gloom. It is honest care for new believers, said by a man still bruised from Lystra. They will not be surprised when trouble comes.
And after they had appointed elders for them in each church, with prayer and fasting they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.

The ministry of the Church was still taking shape, and the titles were not yet fixed as they are today. What is clear already is that the apostles did not leave communities without shepherds, and that they handed them over not to themselves but to the Lord.
how he had opened a door of faith for the Gentiles.
The report is about what God has done, not about the missionaries’ hardships. This verse prepares tomorrow’s question: on what terms do the Gentiles come in?
ch: Pope Benedict XVI took the title of his letter announcing the Year of Faith, Porta Fidei (2011), from this verse: the door of faith is always open for us. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the apostles took care to appoint successors so that the mission entrusted to them would continue (Lumen Gentium 20). Paul’s return to the towns that had stoned him shows the heart of a shepherd: the new believers mattered more to him than his own safety.

r.h: My peace I give to you
set: The Last Supper discourse continues. Peace, shalom, was the ordinary greeting and farewell among Jews. Jesus takes the everyday word and fills it: his peace is the wholeness that comes from God, and he gives it on the night he is to be betrayed. After the resurrection his first word to the disciples will be “Peace be with you” (20:19).
str: v. 27: the gift of peace; do not be troubled.
v. 28: “I am going to the Father”.
v. 29: he tells them beforehand so that they may believe.
vv. 30–31a: the ruler of this world has no power over him; he does what the Father commands.
kw: The Greek word carries the Hebrew shalom: not only the absence of war but wholeness, harmony with God and others.
Used of water stirred up. John uses it of Jesus himself, troubled at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33) and at the approach of his hour (12:27; 13:21). He who was troubled for us gives us his peace.
John’s name for the devil (12:31; 16:11). He is coming in the betrayal and the arrest, but he has no hold on Jesus, who goes to the Cross out of love and obedience.
vv: I do not give to you as the world gives.
The world’s peace often depends on circumstances, or on keeping trouble away. His peace remains even in trouble, because it comes from him.
because the Father is greater than I.
See the question below. Jesus wants the disciples to rejoice that he is going home to the Father, not to cling to him for themselves.
He has no power over me;
Literally “in me he has nothing”. There is nothing in Jesus that belongs to the evil one. His death will not be a defeat but an offering.
ch: In the Roman Mass, before the sign of peace, the priest prays: “Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles: Peace I leave you, my peace I give you”. So this verse is heard at every Mass, and the peace we give one another flows from the Lord’s own gift, not from our feelings. St Augustine teaches that the Father is greater than the Son in the “form of a servant” that the Son took, while in the form of God the Son is equal to the Father (in substance).

qa: If Jesus is God, how can he say “the Father is greater than I”?

The Church confesses the Son as one in being with the Father. Fathers such as St Augustine read this verse of the Son’s human nature: as man, he is less than the Father. Others also saw in it the Father as the source from whom the Son eternally receives all that he is, without being any less God. Either way, the verse speaks of the Son’s love and obedience, not of a lesser divinity.
study: When trouble comes, do I take it as a sign that God has abandoned me, or as part of the road Paul spoke of?
Next time I give the sign of peace at Mass, whom do I most need to give it to in my heart?
